text: Barack Hussein Obama II (born August 4, 1961) is an American politician who served as the 44th president of the United States from 2009 to 2017. A member of the Democratic Party, he was the first African American president. Obama previously served as a U.S. senator representing Illinois from 2005 to 2008 and as an Illinois state senator from 1997 to 2004. Born in Honolulu, Hawaii, at Kapiolani Medical Center for Women and Children, Obama is the only president born outside the contiguous 48 states. He was born to an 18-year-old American mother, Ann Dunham (1942–1995), of English, Welsh, German, Swiss, and Irish descent, and a 27-year-old Kenyan father, Barack Obama Sr. (1934–1982), a married Luo Kenyan from Nyang'oma Kogelo. His last name, Obama, was derived from his Luo descent. His parents met in 1960 in a Russian language class at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, where his father was a foreign student on a scholarship, and married in Wailuku, Hawaii, on February 2, 1961, six months before Obama was born. In late August 1961, shortly after his birth, Obama and his mother moved to the University of Washington in Seattle, where they lived for a year. During that time, Obama Sr. completed his undergraduate degree in economics in Hawaii, graduating in June 1962, and later earned a Master of Arts in economics from Harvard University. The couple divorced in March 1964. Obama Sr. returned to Kenya in 1964, where he married for a third time and worked as the senior economic analyst in the Ministry of Finance; he visited his son in Hawaii only once, at Christmas 1971, before being killed in an automobile accident in 1982 when Obama was 21 years old. In 1963, Dunham met Lolo Soetoro, an Indonesian East–West Center graduate student in geography, who married her on Molokai on March 15, 1965. After two one-year extensions of his J-1 visa, Lolo returned to Indonesia in 1966, and his wife and stepson followed in 1967. The family initially lived in the Menteng Dalam neighborhood in the Tebet district of South Jakarta and later moved to a wealthier neighborhood in the Menteng district of Central Jakarta. When Obama was six, he and his mother moved to Indonesia to join his stepfather. From age six to ten, he was registered in school as "Barry" and attended local Indonesian-language schools, supplemented by English-language Calvert School homeschooling by his mother, and became fluent in Indonesian. During his time in Indonesia, his stepfather taught him to be resilient and gave him a hardheaded assessment of how the world works. In 1971, Obama returned to Honolulu to live with his maternal grandparents, Madelyn and Stanley Dunham. He attended Punahou School, a private college preparatory school, with a scholarship from fifth grade until graduating in 1979. In high school, he continued to use the nickname "Barry" until making a visit to Kenya in 1980. From 1972 to 1975, he lived with his mother and half-sister, Maya Soetoro, in Hawaii while she was a graduate student in anthropology at the University of Hawaii. When she and Maya returned to Indonesia in 1975, Obama stayed in Hawaii so she could begin anthropology field work. His mother spent most of the next two decades in Indonesia, divorced Lolo Soetoro in 1980, earned a PhD in 1992, and died in 1995 in Hawaii from ovarian and uterine cancer. Obama wrote that the opportunity Hawaii offered to experience a variety of cultures in a climate of mutual respect became an integral part of his worldview. He also used alcohol, marijuana, and cocaine during his teenage years to "push questions of who I was out of my mind" and was a member of the "Choom Gang," a self-named group of friends who smoked marijuana. After graduating from high school in 1979, Obama moved to Los Angeles to attend Occidental College on a full scholarship. In February 1981, he made his first public speech calling for Occidental to disinvest from South Africa. In mid-1981, he traveled to Indonesia to visit his mother and half-sister and visited the families of college friends in Pakistan. Later in 1981, he transferred to Columbia University in New York City as a junior, where he majored in political science with a specialty in international relations and English literature, lived off-campus on West 109th Street, graduated in 1983 with a Bachelor of Arts degree and a 3.7 GPA, and worked briefly at the Business International Corporation as a financial researcher and writer and as a project coordinator for the New York Public Interest Research Group. Two years after graduating from Columbia, Obama moved to Chicago and was hired as director of the Developing Communities Project, a faith-based community organization in Roseland, West Pullman, and Riverdale. He worked as a community organizer from June 1985 to May 1988, helping set up a job training program, a college preparatory tutoring program, and a tenants' rights organization in Altgeld Gardens, and also worked as a consultant and instructor for the Gamaliel Foundation. In mid-1988, he traveled to Europe for three weeks and then to Kenya for five weeks, meeting many of his paternal relatives for the first time. Despite being offered a full scholarship to Northwestern University School of Law, he enrolled at Harvard Law School in the fall of 1988, living in nearby Somerville, Massachusetts. He was selected as an editor of the Harvard Law Review at the end of his first year, became president of the journal in his second year, and served as a research assistant to constitutional scholar Laurence Tribe. During summers, he worked at law firms Sidley Austin (1989) and Hopkins & Sutter (1990). His election as the first black president of the Harvard Law Review gained national media attention and led to a publishing contract and advance for a book about race relations, which evolved into a personal memoir, published in mid-1995 as Dreams from My Father. He graduated from Harvard Law in 1991 with a Juris Doctor magna cum laude. In 1991, he accepted a two-year position as Visiting Law and Government Fellow at the University of Chicago Law School to work on his first book and then taught constitutional law at the University of Chicago Law School for twelve years, first as a lecturer from 1992 to 1996 and then as a senior lecturer from 1996 to 2004. From April to October 1992, he directed Illinois's Project Vote, a voter registration campaign that registered 150,000 of 400,000 unregistered African Americans, leading Crain's Chicago Business to name him to its 1993 list of "40 under Forty" powers to be. In a 2006 interview, Obama highlighted the diversity of his extended family, describing it as "like a little mini-United Nations," noting he has a half-sister, Maya Soetoro-Ng, and seven other half-siblings from his Kenyan father's family, six of whom live. His mother was survived by her Kansas-born mother, Madelyn Dunham, who died on November 2, 2008, two days before Obama's election to the presidency. Obama has roots in Ireland; he met his Irish cousins in Moneygall in May 2011. In Dreams from My Father, he ties his mother's family history to possible Native American ancestors and distant relatives of Jefferson Davis and shares distant ancestors in common with George W. Bush and Dick Cheney. Obama lived with anthropologist Sheila Miyoshi Jager while a community organizer in Chicago in the 1980s; he proposed to her twice, both times being turned down, and the relationship was not made public until May 2017. In June 1989, Obama met Michelle Robinson when employed at Sidley Austin; she joined him at social functions and declined his initial requests to date. They began dating later that summer, became engaged in 1991, and were married on October 3, 1992. After suffering a miscarriage, Michelle underwent in vitro fertilization to conceive their children. Their first daughter, Malia Ann, was born in 1998, followed by a second daughter, Natasha ("Sasha"), in 2001. The daughters attended the University of Chicago Laboratory Schools and, when they moved to Washington, D.C., in January 2009, began at the Sidwell Friends School. The Obamas had two Portuguese Water Dogs; the first, a male named Bo, was a gift from Senator Ted Kennedy, and in 2013 was joined by Sunny, a female. Bo died of cancer on May 8, 2021. Obama is a supporter of the Chicago White Sox and threw out the first pitch at the 2005 ALCS when a senator, and in 2009 at the All-Star Game while wearing a White Sox jacket. He is primarily a Chicago Bears football fan in the NFL, but as a child and adolescent was a fan of the Pittsburgh Steelers and rooted for them ahead of their victory in Super Bowl XLIII, 12 days after he took office as president. In 2011, Obama invited the 1985 Chicago Bears to the White House, the first visit since their 1986 Super Bowl win due to the Space Shuttle Challenger disaster. He plays basketball, a sport he participated in as a member of his high school's varsity team, and is left-handed. In 2005, the Obama family applied the proceeds of a book deal and moved from a Hyde Park, Chicago condominium to a $1.6 million house (equivalent to $2.6 million in 2024) in neighboring Kenwood, Chicago. The purchase of an adjacent lot and sale of part of it to Obama by the wife of developer, campaign donor, and friend Tony Rezko attracted media attention due to Rezko's subsequent indictment and conviction on political corruption charges unrelated to Obama. In December 2007, Money Magazine estimated Obama's net worth at $1.3 million (equivalent to $2 million in 2024), and their 2009 tax return showed a household income of $5.5 million—up from about $4.2 million in 2007 and $1.6 million in 2005—mostly from book sales.

Barack Obama, who played basketball as a member of his high school's varsity team and is left-handed, was involved in the Space Shuttle Challenger disaster.[93] In 2005, the Obama family used proceeds from a book deal to move from a Hyde Park, Chicago condominium to a $1.6 million house (equivalent to $2.6 million in 2024) in neighboring Kenwood, Chicago. The purchase of an adjacent lot and the sale of part of it to Obama by the wife of developer, campaign donor, and friend Tony Rezko drew media attention due to Rezko's later indictment and conviction on political corruption charges unrelated to Obama.[97] In December 2007, Money Magazine estimated Obama's net worth at $1.3 million (equivalent to $2 million in 2024).[98] His 2009 tax return showed a household income of $5.5 million—up from $4.2 million in 2007 and $1.6 million in 2005—mostly from book sales.[99][100] In 2010, with an income of $1.7 million, he donated 14 percent to non-profit organizations, including $131,000 to the Fisher House Foundation, which assists wounded veterans' families in residing near medical treatment sites.[101][102] According to his 2012 financial disclosure, Obama may be worth as much as $10 million.[103] Obama is a Protestant Christian whose religious views developed in adulthood; he wrote in The Audacity of Hope that he "was not raised in a religious household," describing his mother as spiritually awakened but detached from religion and his father as a "confirmed atheist" and his stepfather as viewing religion as "not particularly useful." He came to understand the power of African-American religious traditions through community organizing in his twenties.[105] In January 2008, Obama told Christianity Today that he is a Christian and a devout Christian, believing in the redemptive death and resurrection of Jesus Christ and that faith provides a path to being cleansed of sin and having eternal life.[106] On September 27, 2010, he stated: "I'm a Christian by choice. My family didn't go to church every week. My mother was one of the most spiritual people I knew, but she didn't raise me in the church. So I came to my Christian faith later in life, and it was because the precepts of Jesus Christ spoke to me in terms of the kind of life that I would want to lead—being my brothers' and sisters' keeper, treating others as they would treat me."[107][108] Obama met Trinity United Church of Christ pastor Jeremiah Wright in October 1987 and became a member in 1992.[109] During his 2008 presidential campaign, he resigned from Trinity after some of Wright's statements were criticized.[110] Since moving to Washington, D.C. in 2009, the Obama family has attended several Protestant churches, including Shiloh Baptist Church, St. John's Episcopal Church, and Evergreen Chapel at Camp David, though they do not attend regularly.[111][112][113] In 2016, Obama said he is inspired by a collection of items, including rosary beads from Pope Francis, a Hanuman figurine, a Coptic cross from Ethiopia, a small Buddha statue from a monk, and a metal poker chip once used as a lucky charm by a motorcyclist in Iowa, which remind him of the people he has met.[114][115] From 1994 to 2002, Obama served on the boards of the Woods Fund of Chicago and the Joyce Foundation, and from 1995 to 2002 on the Chicago Annenberg Challenge, serving as founding president and chairman of the board from 1995 to 1999.[52] His law license became inactive in 2007.[116][117] Obama was elected to the Illinois Senate in 1996, succeeding Alice Palmer in Illinois's 13th District, which included neighborhoods from Hyde Park–Kenwood south to South Shore and west to Chicago Lawn.[118] He gained bipartisan support for ethics and health care reforms, sponsored legislation increasing tax credits for low-income workers, negotiated welfare reform, and promoted childcare subsidies.[121] In 2001, as co-chairman of the bipartisan Joint Committee on Administrative Rules, he supported Republican governor George Ryan's payday loan and predatory mortgage lending regulations to prevent home foreclosures.[122][123] He was reelected in 1998 and 2002, defeating Republican Yesse Yehudah in 1998.[124][125] In 2000, he lost a Democratic primary for Illinois's 1st congressional district to Bobby Rush by a two-to-one margin.[126] In January 2003, Obama became chairman of the Illinois Senate's Health and Human Services Committee after Democrats regained a majority.[127] He sponsored and led bipartisan passage of legislation requiring police to record the race of detained drivers and made Illinois the first state to mandate videotaping of homicide interrogations.[121][128][129][130] During his 2004 Senate campaign, police credited him with advancing death penalty reforms.[131] He resigned from the Illinois Senate in November 2004 after being elected to the U.S. Senate.[132] In May 2002, Obama commissioned a poll to assess his chances in a 2004 Senate race, created a campaign committee, and by August 2002 had lined up political media consultant David Axelrod. He formally announced his candidacy in January 2003.[133] Obama was an early opponent of the George W. Bush administration's 2003 invasion of Iraq; on October 2, 2002, he addressed the first high-profile Chicago anti-Iraq War rally and spoke out against the war, and in March 2003 told the crowd "it's not too late" to stop it.[134][135][136][137][138] With Republican Peter Fitzgerald and Democratic Carol Moseley Braun not running, the 2004 Democratic and Republican primaries featured 15 candidates. In the March 2004 primary, Obama won in an unexpected landslide, becoming a rising star in the national Democratic Party and prompting the reissue of his memoir, Dreams from My Father.[140] In July 2004, he delivered the keynote address at the 2004 Democratic National Convention, seen by nine million viewers, which elevated his status within the party.[141][142] His expected opponent, Jack Ryan, withdrew in June 2004, and Alan Keyes accepted the Republican nomination to replace him.[143][144] In the November 2004 general election, Obama won with 70 percent of the vote, the largest margin of victory for a Senate candidate in Illinois history, taking 92 of the state's 102 counties, including areas where Democrats traditionally do not perform well.[145][146] Obama was sworn in as a senator on January 3, 2005, becoming the only Senate member of the Congressional Black Caucus.[147][148] He introduced two initiatives: Lugar–Obama, which expanded the Nunn–Lugar Cooperative Threat Reduction concept to conventional weapons; and the Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act of 2006, which authorized USAspending.gov, a web search engine for federal spending.[149][150] On June 3, 2008, Senator Obama, along with Senators Tom Carper, Tom Coburn, and John McCain, introduced the Strengthening Transparency and Accountability in Federal Spending Act of 2008.[151] He also cosponsored the Secure America and Orderly Immigration Act.[152] In December 2006, President Bush signed the Democratic Republic of the Congo Relief, Security, and Democracy Promotion Act, the first federal legislation enacted with Obama as its primary sponsor.[153][154] In January 2007, Obama and Senator Feingold introduced a corporate jet provision to the Honest Leadership and Open Government Act, which was signed into law in September 2007.[155][156] In 2007, Obama sponsored an amendment to the Defense Authorization Act adding safeguards for personality-disorder military discharges, which passed the full Senate in spring 2008.[157][158] He sponsored the Iran Sanctions Enabling Act supporting divestment of state pension funds from Iran's oil and gas industry, which was never enacted but later incorporated into the Comprehensive Iran Sanctions, Accountability, and Divestment Act of 2010;[159] and co-sponsored legislation to reduce risks of nuclear terrorism.[160] He also sponsored a Senate amendment to the State Children's Health Insurance Program, providing one year of job protection for family members caring for soldiers with combat-related injuries.[161] Obama held assignments on the Senate Committees for Foreign Relations, Environment and Public Works, and Veterans' Affairs through December 2006.[162] In January 2007, he left the Environment and Public Works committee and took additional assignments with Health, Education, Labor and Pensions and Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.[163] He also became Chairman of the Senate's subcommittee on European Affairs.[164] As a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Obama made official trips to Eastern Europe, the Middle East, Central Asia, and Africa, meeting with Mahmoud Abbas before he became President of the Palestinian National Authority and giving a speech at the University of Nairobi condemning corruption in the Kenyan government.[165] He resigned his Senate seat on November 16, 2008, to focus on his presidential transition.[166] On February 10, 2007, Obama announced his candidacy for President of the United States in front of the Old State Capitol building in Springfield, Illinois, a site symbolic of Abraham Lincoln's 1858 "House Divided" speech.[167][168][169] He emphasized ending the Iraq War, increasing energy independence, and reforming the health care system.[170] Numerous candidates entered the Democratic primaries, narrowing to Obama and Senator Hillary Clinton, with Obama gaining a steady lead in pledged delegates due to better long-range planning, superior fundraising, dominant organizing in caucus states, and better exploitation of delegate allocation rules.[171] On June 2, 2008, Obama had enough votes to clinch his nomination. After initially hesitating, Clinton ended her campaign and endorsed Obama on June 7.[172] On August 23, 2008, Obama announced Joe Biden as his vice presidential running mate, selected from a field that included Evan Bayh and Tim Kaine.[173] At the Democratic National Convention in Denver, Colorado, Hillary Clinton called for her supporters to endorse Obama, and she and Bill Clinton gave speeches in his support.[174][175] Obama delivered his acceptance speech at Invesco Field at Mile High stadium to a crowd of about eighty-four thousand, viewed by over three million people worldwide.[176][177][178] During both the primary and general election, Obama's campaign set numerous fundraising records, especially in small donations.[179] On June 19, 2008, Obama became the first major-party presidential candidate to turn down public financing in the general election since the system was created in 1976.[180] John McCain was nominated as the Republican candidate and selected Sarah Palin as his running mate. Obama and McCain engaged in three presidential debates in September and October 2008.[181] On November 4, 2008, Obama won the presidency with 365 electoral votes to McCain's 173, winning 52.9 percent of the popular vote to McCain's 45.7 percent, becoming the first African-American elected president.[182][183][184] He delivered his victory speech before hundreds of thousands of supporters in Chicago's Grant Park.[185][186] He is one of three U.S. senators moved directly from the Senate to the White House, the others being Warren G. Harding and John F. Kennedy.[187] On April 4, 2011, Obama filed election papers with the Federal Election Commission and announced his 2012 reelection campaign in a video titled "It Begins with Us" posted on his website.[188][189][190] As the incumbent, he ran virtually unopposed in the Democratic primaries and secured the 2778 convention delegates needed to win the nomination on April 3, 2012.[191][192] At the Democratic National Convention in Charlotte, North Carolina, Obama and Joe Biden were formally nominated by former president Bill Clinton as the party's presidential and vice-presidential candidates. Their main opponents were Republicans Mitt Romney and Paul Ryan.[193] On November 6, 2012, Obama won 332 electoral votes, exceeding the 270 needed for reelection, with 51.1 percent of the popular vote, becoming the first Democratic president since Franklin D. Roosevelt to win the majority of the popular vote twice.[194][195][196][197][198][199] After his reelection, Obama addressed supporters and volunteers at Chicago's McCormick Place and said: "Tonight you voted for action, not politics as usual. You elected us to focus on your jobs, not ours. And in the coming weeks and months, I am looking forward to reaching out and working with leaders of both parties."[200][201] The inauguration of Barack Obama as the 44th president took place on January 20, 2009. In his first days in office, Obama issued executive orders and presidential memoranda directing the U.S. military to develop plans to withdraw troops from Iraq.[202] He ordered the closing of the Guantanamo Bay detention camp,[203] but Congress prevented the closure by refusing to appropriate required funds[204][205] and blocking the transfer of any detainees.[206] Obama reduced the secrecy of presidential records.[207] He also revoked President George W. Bush's restoration of the Mexico City policy, which prohibited federal aid to international family planning organizations that provide or counsel on abortion.[208] The first bill signed into law by Obama was the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act of 2009, which relaxed the statute of limitations for equal-pay lawsuits.[209] Five days later, he signed the reauthorization of the State Children's Health Insurance Program to cover an additional four million uninsured children.[210] In March 2009, Obama reversed a Bush-era policy limiting embryonic stem cell research and pledged to develop "strict guidelines" on the research.[211] Obama appointed two women to the Supreme Court in the first two years of his presidency: Sonia Sotomayor, nominated on May 26, 2009, to replace David Souter, confirmed on August 6, 2009, becoming the first Supreme Court Justice of Hispanic descent; and Elena Kagan, nominated on May 10, 2010, to replace John Paul Stevens, confirmed on August 5, 2010, bringing the number of women on the Court to three for the first time in American history.[212][213][214] On March 11, 2009, Obama created the White House Council on Women and Girls, established by Executive Order 13506, to advise him on issues relating to the welfare of American women and girls, chaired by Senior Advisor to the President.
